evidence_quotes.quote: En cuanto al acceso a los servicios de agua y saneamiento, también se presentan desigualdades según quién sea el prestador de SAS. Las poblaciones donde el prestador principal es una cooperativa, tienen un promedio de acceso a agua por red pública del 80% y del 22% en cloacas. Esta situación contrasta con la realidad de las localidades que son provistas por la empresa estatal, donde el promedio de acceso a agua por red pública es del 90% y el de acceso a cloacas es del 50%.

Por otro lado, debido a que el poder de concesión está a cargo de los Estados locales, las cooperativas, a diferencia de las comunas y municipios, están sujetas a un doble control: por parte de las autoridades locales y por parte del Ente Regulador de los Servicios Sanitarios (ENRESS). Esto diﬁculta los trámites necesarios que debe hacer una cooperativa para poder funcionar, como por ejemplo el pedido de aumento de tarifa.

Está regulado por la Ley 11220/94, que determina un esquema de gestión discriminatorio de los servicios sanitarios, puesto que el Estado provincial está obligado a prestar los servicios de agua y cloacas solamente a 15 localidades, que juntas reúnen el 59% de la población provincial. En las 347 localidades restantes el poder de concesión está a cargo de sus gobiernos locales y el gobierno provincial no está obligado a garantizar con recursos propios que el poblamiento de estas localidades acceda a los SAS

Para completar el período de estudio y tener una mayor comprensión de los tipos de relaciones predominantes, los conﬂictos y los problemas que originan las acciones realizamos entrevistas a actores clave (funcionarios políticos, personal técnico y miembros de organizaciones sociales), analizamos documentos institucionales y relevamos los datos de cobertura de agua y cloacas provistos por el Instituto Nacional de Estadísticas y Censos (INDEC) y por el ENRESS.

Con relación a la cobertura de cloacas la desigualdad es aún más acentuada. Si bien las cooperativas han logrado ampliar la cobertura, pasando de un 22 a un 37%, siguen estando muy por debajo del nivel de cobertura de las localidades provistas por ASSA, que era para el año 2018 de un 68%.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines community/locality-level access to and network coverage of piped drinking water (agua por red pública) and sewerage (cloacas) across localities in Santa Fe Province, Argentina, focusing on the 124 localities supplied by 126 water and sanitation cooperatives compared with the 15 localities supplied by the provincial state utility ASSA.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it clearly examines state action, governance, institutional relationships, and regulatory politics in water and sanitation provision. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, although a substantial part of Section IV tracks broader political-institutional actions and partisan change using Jessop's Strategic-Relational Approach, the study directly analyses concrete rule-type regulatory, ownership, tariff/subsidy, and discretionary-allocation mechanisms governing service access: (1) Provincial Law 11220/94's bifurcated utility-ownership and statutory obligation/subsidy rules (mandating provincial provision and 40% operating subsidies for majority state-owned utility ASSA in 15 localities, while leaving 347 localities under municipal/communal concession without statutory provincial subsidies); (2) dual regulatory control over cooperatives by both local concessioning authorities and the provincial regulator ENRESS, which complicates administrative procedures such as tariff-increase requests and limits cost-recovery financing for sewer networks; (3) discretionary, non-systematic provincial infrastructure interventions; and (4) failed legislative bills to reform Law 11220 over stripping ENRESS of tariff and regulatory powers.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical exploratory mixed/qualitative-descriptive case study combining: (1) a media event-reconstruction database of 48 cooperative-related news articles (115 coded actions in 2010-2011, selected from 683 articles in La Capital and El Litoral across 2007-2015); (2) key-informant interviews with provincial water officials, regulators, cooperative leaders, consumer organizations, and legislators; (3) analysis of statutory/legislative and planning documents; and (4) descriptive analysis of census and regulatory water/sewer coverage statistics from INDEC (2010) and ENRESS (2016, 2019). Qualitative/descriptive socio-legal and institutional studies are eligible for the systematic review even without a meta-analysable effect estimate.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports locality/subsystem-level service access and availability outcomes, specifically percentage coverage of piped public drinking water networks and sewerage networks in cooperative-served localities versus ASSA-served localities in 2010 and 2018 (water coverage: 80% to 92% in cooperatives vs. 90% to 95% in ASSA; sewer coverage: 22% to 37% in cooperatives vs. 50% to 68% in ASSA), alongside the breakdown of water versus sewerage service provision across cooperatives and local governments.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (localities/provider subsystems in Santa Fe Province — 124 localities served by 126 cooperatives vs. 15 localities served by ASSA — plus 115 coded institutional/civil-society actions in 2010-2011), exposure (Law 11220/94's bifurcated utility-ownership, subsidy, and dual-regulation regime alongside post-2007 provincial executive action and failed regulatory reform), outcome (piped water and sewer network coverage in 2010 and 2018 and service-provision mix), and study design (exploratory empirical case study using newspaper action coding, key-informant interviews, document analysis, and descriptive administrative/census statistics) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: The full text is in Spanish (with English title and abstract). Per Inclusion Criterion 10 and Checklist item 6, non-English/Portuguese/Dutch studies are eligible when translation from the provided full text is feasible and the study is potentially important; machine-readable full text is complete and directly translatable, so translation method and translator should be logged in extraction_note upon data extraction.

study_design: Exploratory empirical case study (mixed qualitative-descriptive design combining newspaper event/action coding, key-informant interviews, institutional/legislative document analysis, and descriptive comparison of census and regulatory coverage data from 2010 to 2018)
population_and_sample: Localities and water/sanitation provider subsystems in Santa Fe Province, Argentina (362 districts total, focusing on 124 localities served by 126 cooperatives compared with 15 localities served by state utility ASSA), alongside 115 coded state and civil-society actions from 48 newspaper articles (2010-2011, drawn from 683 articles in 2007-2015) and key-informant interviews.
exposure: Bifurcated statutory utility-ownership, subsidy, and regulatory regime under Santa Fe Provincial Law 11220/94 (subsidized majority state-owned utility ASSA serving 15 localities vs. unsubsidized cooperatives in 124 localities under local concession and dual local/ENRESS regulatory oversight over tariffs and operations), discretionary post-2007 provincial executive infrastructure interventions, and stalled legislative reform of Law 11220/ENRESS powers.
outcome: Locality/subsystem-level percentage coverage of piped public drinking water networks and sewerage networks (2010 and 2018, INDEC and ENRESS), cooperative versus municipal water/sewer provision shares, and institutional/regulatory conflict over service provision and tariff/regulatory oversight.
rationale: This Spanish-language empirical study (eligible per Criterion 10 as translation from the full text is straightforward) satisfies all systematic-review inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Using newspaper action-event coding (115 actions), key-informant interviews, statutory/legislative document analysis, and 2010-2018 INDEC/ENRESS coverage data, it examines how Provincial Law 11220/94's bifurcated utility-ownership and subsidy structure (40% operating subsidies and direct state provision via ASSA in 15 localities vs. zero statutory provincial subsidies and dual municipal/ENRESS regulatory control over tariff increases and operations for 126 cooperatives in 124 localities), discretionary executive infrastructure works, and failed regulatory reform of ENRESS govern persistent disparities in piped drinking water (92% vs. 95% in 2018) and sewerage network coverage (37% vs. 68% in 2018).
